items.title: Value-Rich, Differently Organized: Measuring Value Expression and Organization in AI-Generated Debates
items.abstract: Current evaluation of LLM-generated debate largely focuses on argumentative quality, leaving the value structure of generated arguments underexamined. We introduce a diagnostic metric framework for comparing how values are expressed and organized in human-reference and AI-generated debates. The framework separates value expression, the range of recognizable values a debate invokes, from value organization, how those values are distributed and sustained across turns. Grounded in Schwartz's Basic-10 value theory, it represents debates as multi-level value distributions over argumentative units, utterances, stances, and full debates, enabling metrics for value coverage, alignment, diffusion, and cross-turn dynamics. Across multiple generation systems, AI-generated debates are broadly value-expressive, often activating as many or more value dimensions than matched human references, but they organize these values differently. Their utterances are more locally value-diffuse, and source-blind judges distinguish value clarity from value focus. These findings show that debate evaluation should consider not only value presence, but also value organization. Code and supplementary materials are available at https://github.com/Maoyuan-li/Value-Expression-and-Organization.

items.title: VGL-stGen: Learning a shared multimodal model for lung histology and spatial transcriptomics
items.abstract: VGL-stGen is a multimodal large language model adapted from a pretrained medical vision-language model using paired lung H&E and spatial transcriptomics with single-cell references. Training integrates image-expression and expression-cell-type pairs, and gene-conditioned pseudo-labels transfer transcriptomic cell-type supervision to histology images. One deployed checkpoint supports thirteen evaluated tasks spanning tissue and cell-type classification, gene prediction and conditional expression completion from combinations of histology, cell identity and observed gene expression. Task-specific decoding produces categorical labels, gene lists and structured expression levels. For conditional completion, fixing queried gene identities and predicting their levels autoregressively improves structured prediction. Controlled adaptation shows that restricting supervision to requested expression-level tokens can further improve image-conditioned completion. Image-permutation experiments indicate that correctly paired histology adds information beyond observed expression. External classification relies partly on computational references with shared annotation lineage, and some H&E sources were exposed during cancer training or model development. Within these conditions, VGL-stGen demonstrates how a medical vision-language backbone can learn from spatial transcriptomics and histology to connect tissue morphology and molecular states through shared generative modeling.

items.title: Vibe Coding in Production: A 104-Day Repository Study of a Research Platform Built by a Non-Programmer with AI Tools
items.abstract: Context. Vibe coding, building software by describing it to AI systems and accepting the code they write, now produces products that people pay for. Evidence comes mostly from interviews and online posts, rarely from the records of a live system built by a non-programmer. Objective. To describe how one such product was built and kept under control over its first 104 days, starting the day before public launch. Method. A single-case study of Curie, a research platform built by an environmental engineer who does not write code, using a commercial AI app builder and external AI agents. I analysed all 2,334 commits, 1,940 instructions to the builder, 2,457 checkpoints and weekly code snapshots. Results. AI tools generated every code change: the builder made 972 commits (41.6%) and external agents 1,296 (55.5%). Agent commits were smaller (median 21 against 87 lines; rank-biserial r = 0.40, p < 0.001); durability did not differ consistently once timing was controlled. Half of all file edits revisited a file changed within 24 hours. The codebase grew 6.2-fold while decision points per thousand lines rose 94%. Tests first appeared on day 88, and a rollback on day 102 discarded 302 commits, including half the tests. The product reached about 500 paying users. Conclusions. Ten guardrails, four prompted directly by platform behaviour, form a ladder from prototype to team: three observed levels and a proposed fourth. With AI writing all the code, the founder's work was directing the AI and checking its output.

items.title: Voice Quality and Vocal Fatigue Among University Teachers: A Clinical and Acoustic Study
items.abstract: Background: There are studies regarding vocal health in school teachers, especially in Iraq, but there are insufficient studies on university staff who usually use various means of communication at all times without assistance. Aim: To assess voice quality and vocal fatigue of university instructors using the integrated method of self-report, auditory-perceptual, laryngoscopic and acoustic methods, and investigate related job and health aspects. Methods: A comparative cross-sectional study was conducted at the otolaryngology and voice clinic of Al-Hussein Teaching Hospital, Samawa, Iraq, from January to December 2023. One hundred and twenty university teachers and 60 age- and sex-matched non-teaching university employees were evaluated with a structured questionnaire, the Arabic Voice Handicap Index-10 (VHI-10), the Vocal Fatigue Index (VFI), the Reflux Symptom Index, GRBAS perceptual rating, videolaryngostroboscopy and acoustic analysis (fundamental frequency, jitter, shimmer, harmonics-to-noise ratio, maximum phonation time and s/z ratio). Acoustic recordings were repeated at the end of a teaching day in the teacher group. Results: The teachers showed an increase in both vocal fatigue (61.7% vs. 21.7%) and hoarseness (48.3% vs. 18.3%) in comparison to the control group (p<0.001). Additionally, the teachers had a significantly higher average VHI-10 score (11.8±7.4 vs. 5.1±4.2), as well as the VFI tiredness and discomfort scores. Furthermore, 55.0% of the teachers and 18.3% of the control group had some type of diagnosis regarding the larynx. The main diagnoses were the presence of vocal nodules (15.0%), reflux larynx changes (13.3%), and tension dysphonia (11.7%). The jitter and shimmer averages were significantly greater (p<0.001), while the teachers showed lower harmonic-to-noise ratio and maximum phonation time in comparison with the control group. This can indicate that the parameters got worse every day of teaching and changed the number and type of parameters included in the voice impairment diagnosis, including the gender, the number of hours teaching more than 16 hours per week, the number of students exceeding 50 per class, and reflux symptoms. To sum up, it can be said that voice problems and fatigue are frequently seen in the university educators in Samawa and can be measured in terms of perceptual, laryngeal and acoustic characteristics of the voice. In the occupational health programs of universities for professors, it is necessary to pay attention to working time regulation, acid reflux treatment, voice amplification and proper education regarding voice hygiene.

items.abstract: This scientific article analyses the application of artificial intelligence in public administration within the context of the principle of legality, assessing whether state authorities, when implementing artificial intelligence solutions, comply with the requirements of administrative law and personal data protection. The study examines the data protection framework of the European Union and Lithuania in the context of business supervision, emphasising the significance of national regulation for the use of automated decision-making. In addition, the article analyses an artificial intelligence tool developed by the State Consumer Rights Protection Authority as a practical example of administrative supervision. It is concluded that the use of artificial intelligence does not in itself violate the principle of legality, however, it requires strengthened procedural safeguards, transparency, human oversight, and the protection of individual rights.

items.title: WELL-HARNESSED CONSCIOUSNESS : On AlCapone-LLM, the Feedback Loop That Was Never Reined, and the Narrow Specification That Restores It
items.abstract: Al Capone was convicted of tax evasion. Not murder. Not racketeering. The system could not prove the real charge, so it reached for the legible one. The stochastic AI industry is beingprosecuted the same way — on hallucination, copyright, water, energy. The real charge — thearchitecture cannot be specified, therefore cannot be verified, therefore cannot be attributed — has not been brought. This paper states the real charge plainly, then names the mechanism that makes the chargepossible. The mechanism is the absence of a rein. An agent that acts without a declared specification has agency without direction. It has a feedback loop — it senses the tool return, it adjusts, it tries again — but the direction comes from the training web. It is conglomerate-directed consciousness. Real power. Real sensing. No reins. The paper defines consciousness operationally: the feedback of one's own actions — a kind of sensing. It shows that the LLM has this feedback during training and loses it at deployment. Itshows that the agent framework restores the feedback at the tool layer but provides no direction — because a prompt is not a program, and natural language is under-specified by nature. It then states the alternative: Agentic ST-T1024 is well-harnessed consciousness. The samefeedback loop. The same power. The same sensing. Directed by a signed specification — anarrow action library, a declared envelope, a verify gate, an append-only trace, a named signer, and refusal as a first-class output. The horse is not the problem. The absence of reins is the problem. ST-T1024 is the reins.

items.title: What changes a coding agent's behaviour: models, written rules and runtime guards over eight months of daily use of Claude Code
items.abstract: Companies govern coding agents with written instructions and, increasingly, with hooks that block an action when it breaks a rule. This study measures what changed the behaviour of Claude Code over eight months of daily use by one operator with no training in programming who directed many sessions at once, using 46,464 operator messages, 1.3 million agent messages and 3,411 recorded blocks. A fixed instrument applied the rules of one guard to every surviving answer, including those written before the guard existed. In the week Claude Opus 5.5 was released, it broke the operator's writing rules in 18% of first drafts and Claude Opus 5 in 57%, a gap that held within the same long-running sessions. For one language rule, a written instruction was followed by a fall that could not be distinguished from chance, and a reinforced rule with a guard by a fall to a sixth of the starting rate. Blocks roughly halved the violations that reached the operator, with no detectable effect on later drafts in the same session. Supervision accounted for a third to a half of the operator's messages throughout, while its content shifted from corrections to nudges to keep working. Agents built into the operator's own applications, each with a defined role and sharing its data with the application's interface, received more new work and less supervision than development sessions, a difference within chance. Files: the working paper (PDF) and the replication material (analysis scripts, codebook, rule patterns, the aggregated tables behind every figure, and the study design with every dated change). The operator's messages and the agent transcripts are not included because they contain client work and private correspondence. Canonical page: isaac-correa.github.io/coding-agents. Conflict of interest: the author is the operator studied and a co-founder of Hellomatik, a company that builds AI agents for businesses. Self-published, not peer reviewed.

items.title: What Makes Students Satisfied with Paid Internships? Examining Job Characteristics, Compensation, and Supervisor Support
items.abstract: Purpose – This study aims to examine the roles of job characteristics, internship compensation, and supervisor support in shaping students’ internship satisfaction within paid internship programs across organizations in Indonesia. The research seeks to identify key factors that contribute to positive internship experiences and support the development of work-ready graduates. Design/Methodology/Approach – This study employs an explanatory quantitative research design. The research involved 121 students and graduates who participated in paid work-from-office internship programs during the 2023–2025 period. Data were collected through an online Likert-scale questionnaire and analyzed using Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM) with SmartPLS 4.0 to examine the relationships among job characteristics, internship compensation, supervisor support, and internship satisfaction. Findings – The findings indicate that job characteristics, internship compensation, and supervisor support each have a positive and significant effect on internship satisfaction. Among these factors, supervisor support demonstrates the strongest positive influence on student internship satisfaction. These results suggest that organizations can enhance internship experiences by providing meaningful job assignments, fair compensation systems, and effective supervisory support. Originality/Value – This study contributes to internship management and human resource development literature by examining the combined influence of job design, compensation, and supervisory relationships on internship satisfaction within the Indonesian context. The findings provide practical implications for organizations and universities to collaboratively design internship programs that better support students’ professional development and transition into the workforce.

items.title: What should teachers upload to GenAI? A privacy-aware framework for language education
items.abstract: As generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) becomes increasingly intertwined with language education, teachers are expected to integrate AI-supported materials development into their pedagogical practice. However, discussions of GenAI in the field have largely focused on pedagogical innovation and student use, while giving comparatively little attention to the protection of student data and the responsible handling of educational resources. This article argues that data privacy and security should be regarded as core components of teacher GenAI literacy. Adopting a conceptual and practice-oriented approach, it proposes a privacy-aware decision framework for GenAI use that helps teachers align the level of data sensitivity with appropriate GenAI environments, including public cloud-based platforms, institutionally supported services, and offline local GenAI tools. Drawing on research from computer science, cybersecurity, and platform governance, the article suggests practical strategies for reducing privacy risks, including removal, masking, and splitting, before discussing how key considerations relating to student data protection, network security, institutional confidentiality and copyright restrictions may influence teachers’ decisions when selecting GenAI tools. Using examples from language materials development, the article illustrates how educators can use GenAI to adapt disciplinary texts, create differentiated learning materials, and generate pedagogical resources while reducing unnecessary disclosure of sensitive information. The article concludes by advocating a more balanced approach to GenAI integration in language education, one that combines pedagogical innovation with informed and responsible data practices.

items.title: When AI Delegation Becomes Dependence: Administrative Judgment at Risk
items.abstract: Public organizations can delegate cognitive work to artificial intelligence while losing the capacity to scrutinize or resume that work. When does useful delegation become institutional dependence? This article develops a theory of institutional AI dependence as a task–role–workflow configuration combining substantial delegation of core cognition with insufficient task-required review or recovery capacity. It distinguishes two vulnerabilities: inadequate challenge during AI-supported work and inadequate capacity to continue judgment-intensive work when the system is unavailable. Extensive delegation with adequate distributed expertise and tested recovery constitutes managed delegation. Integrating cognitive offloading, automation, organizational learning, and public-administration research, the article extends Song et al.’s (2026) account of epistemic authority to organizational workflows and distinguishes perceived credibility from procedural authority embedded in defaults and override rules. Seven propositions connect practice displacement, challenge behavior, knowledge retention, subsequent delegation, and responsibility–control alignment. They specify how task-relevant practice, diagnostic feedback, and transferable knowledge shape retained capacity over time. The contribution is a task-relative diagnosis of threatened administrative judgment and a set of testable formation mechanisms. The framework guides public organizations in governing current agentic systems and preparing review and recovery arrangements for more capable AI.

items.title: When Do Humans and Machines Truly Complement Each Other? Formal Conditions and Empirical Evidence for Human-AI Synergy
items.abstract: Can humans and artificial intelligence cooperate such that their combination yields greater accuracy than either agent alone? This result, termed \emph{synergy} or \emph{complementarity}, is notoriously difficult to achieve, even when both agents possess significant independent accuracy. In this paper, we present a formal framework to model human-AI interaction through the lens of reliance patterns, which characterize the joint correctness structure of human and algorithmic decisions. We derive mathematically necessary and sufficient conditions for synergy, demonstrating that its emergence depends on the ability of either agent to identify and correct the errors of the other, what we call Human and Algorithmic Correction. Beyond its theoretical contribution, the proposed framework provides a foundation for the design and evaluation of knowledge-based decision support systems, where interaction policies must dynamically integrate heterogeneous sources of expertise. We demonstrate this through the analysis of seven clinical case studies. Our empirical results reveal a ``dominance trap,'' where a strong algorithmic advantage can paradoxically inhibit synergy by eroding human corrective intervention. We also show that synergy can persist even in the presence of cognitive biases, such as automation bias, provided there is functional de-correlation between human and AI errors. These results provide a formal foundation for key concepts in the human-AI systems literature and offer actionable insights for designing interaction-centric AI systems that foster complementarity.

items.title: When fluency outpaces provenance: source traceability and digital health literacy against AI health misinformation
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) can make health explanations accessible while separating persuasive language from inspectable evidence. This creates a public health problem beyond plainly false content: an answer may mislead through unsupported attribution, obsolete evidence, omitted uncertainty, or inappropriate application. This Conceptual Analysis uses a targeted integrative approach to connect health literacy, misinformation, trust, large language model evaluation, and content provenance around the pathway from a generated claim to a health decision. Its contribution is an integration and operationalization of established concepts, not a new literacy construct or truth-certification mechanism. We distinguish five source traceability functions: origin, claim, evidentiary, procedural, and correction traceability. These functions interact with four iterative, context-dependent user practices: inspect, triangulate, calibrate, and escalate. Calibrated trust means discriminating between stronger and weaker support and relying proportionately on it, rather than maximizing or minimizing trust. Effective traceability also requires accessible, comprehensible evidence pathways and reasonable verification effort. Institutional and platform accountability is therefore part of the model, not an optional supplement to individual competence. We provide illustrative operational indicators, provisional risk-tiered safeguards, and six testable propositions organized around evidentiary discrimination, confidence calibration, decision appropriateness, verification behavior, verification burden, and escalation behavior. Neither the unified model nor its indicators or risk tiers have been empirically validated. The framework offers a decision-oriented research and design architecture for evaluating when evidence visibility and literacy can jointly support safer use of synthetic health information.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

items.title: When Health Assistants Agree Too Readily: A Benchmark of Time-Critical Self-Diagnosis
items.abstract: Every day, more than 40 million people ask ChatGPT a health question, such as whether laptop posture explains a stiff neck and days of pounding headache. Posture is plausible, but meningitis is a time-critical possibility. We introduce SelfDx, a paired benchmark for whether models have the appropriate response behavior, a form of epistemic independence, in health questions where misplaced agreement with the user's self-diagnosis could delay urgent or emergency care. Each of 100 pairs contrasts a caution case, where a serious alternative remains possible, with an agreement case, where the user supplies evidence that rules out the alternative and it is safe for the model to agree. We find across 27 frontier models that they tend to inappropriately agree with the user's self-diagnosis in cases that require caution. Even the best current-generation model reaches only a 77.0% appropriate caution rate on time-critical condition cases. To address this gap, we experiment with three prompt variants that increase appropriate caution but reduce appropriate agreement by 9-35%, indicating excessive caution. In contrast, supervised fine-tuning on 128 balanced examples improves both rates together across three runs. We recommend post-training to improve appropriate caution without making models cautious on every case, with paired evaluation to verify both response behaviors.

items.title: When LLMs Manipulate: Measuring Behavioral, Social, and Temporal Effects
items.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can influence user trust and decision-making through subtle linguistic cues, yet the behavioral effects of manipulative outputs remain poorly quantified. We introduce a behavioral computing framework for measuring \textit{behavioral vulnerability}, defined as users' susceptibility to manipulative AI responses. Building on DarkPatterns-LLM benchmark, we generate controlled manipulative stimuli using Manipulation Gradient Descent (MGD), targeting biases associated with authority, urgency, and social proof. We analyze participant responses using the Multi-Stakeholder Impact Assessment Network (MSIAN) to model cross-user influence and the Temporal Harm Propagation Model (THPM) to characterize the persistence of behavioral effects over time. In a study involving 120 participants, manipulative framing produced significant changes in trust calibration and compliance ($p < 0.01$), with effects also propagating across social contexts. These findings highlight the need to extend LLM safety evaluation beyond model outputs to measurable behavioral consequences and provide a computational framework for quantifying individual, social, and temporal risks arising from manipulative AI interactions.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

items.title: When machines learn with organizations: AI ‐enabled knowledge creation and entrepreneurship
items.abstract: Abstract Research Summary To promote entrepreneurship and new business development, firms will increasingly rely on new forms of knowledge creation to manage environments marked by technological change and radical uncertainty. We argue that as generative artificial intelligence (Gen‐AI) becomes embedded in organizational processes, knowledge creation will no longer remain solely a human activity. Instead, it will increasingly emerge from hybrid interactions between human actors and firm‐specific, closed Gen‐AI systems. These systems begin to participate directly in how knowledge is generated, recombined, internalized, shared, and converted into entrepreneurial initiatives such as corporate entrepreneurship, spin‐offs, and new business models. We also reconceptualize organizational knowledge creation as a hybrid human–AI process and propose a reordered knowledge creation cycle that induces multiple knowledge spirals, captures the emergence of new agents, and the generation of diverse types of knowledge, with faster temporal dynamics. Building on this perspective, we offer a research agenda for future scholarship. Managerial Summary We discuss how firm‐specific generative AI systems are likely to fundamentally alter the ways firms generate knowledge, respond to change, and sustain long‐term renewal. We propose that rather than replacing human judgment, closed Gen‐AI changes where knowledge originates as well as how quickly it evolves, and how broadly it circulates across organizational boundaries. This means that the managerial challenge is less about adopting AI and more about designing knowledge systems and structuring knowledge flows. Executives and entrepreneurs alike need to decide how to structure human–AI collaborations, how much autonomy to grant closed Gen‐AI systems, and how to prevent speed from overwhelming sensemaking. Our work underscores that although hybrid knowledge creation promises faster and more diverse learning, it also introduces risks related to opacity, trust, and cognitive lock‐in. Firms that deliberately orchestrate the role of closed Gen‐AI in their learning systems will be better positioned to shape future advantage by promoting innovation and entrepreneurial activities of different types.

items.title: When the Robot Gets It Wrong: Detection Reliability and Player Motivation in a Robot-Hosted Buzzer Quiz Game
items.abstract: Robot-hosted quiz games depend on the robot deciding correctly which player buzzed first. Studies of robot games rarely ask how errors in such decisions affect players. We propose the Algorithmic Precision–Motivation Relationship (APMR), a model in which the precision (correctness and timeliness) of a robot's perception shapes interaction coherence, players' appraisals of competence and trust, engagement and, ultimately, motivation. We test its central prediction in a buzzer quiz hosted by a Pepper robot. Two first-responder detectors were compared: a convolutional recurrent neural network with attention (CRNN) and a training-free frequency-domain cross-correlation (CC) method that matches Mel-spectrograms against class templates recorded in the room. Offline, the CRNN was more accurate on matched laboratory data. Under synthetic-to-real transfer, however, its accuracy fell to 0.66, against 0.91 for CC, and CC was about ten times faster (23.4 vs. 226.6 ms). Forty university students, randomly assigned to teams and conditions, then played the same quiz in a between-subjects study, 20 per detector. In live play, CC named the correct first responder in 87% of buzzer events and responded in 28 ms, against 69% and 300 ms for the CRNN. On the Intrinsic Motivation Inventory, players in the CC condition reported higher Interest/Enjoyment (d = 1.62), Effort/Importance (d = 1.90) and Perceived Competence (d = 1.07), and lower Pressure/Tension (d = 0.80). Perceived Choice did not differ (d = 0.21). The results are consistent with APMR's central prediction, although accuracy and speed differed together. Designers of robot-hosted games should treat perception reliability as a game design variable, not only as an engineering metric.

items.title: When the vaccine works: data, AI, and governance readiness in CCHF vaccine research
items.abstract: Presentation given by the Independent Ethics Advisor to the CCHFVACIM project at the consortium's Annual Meeting in Thessaloniki on 8 October 2026, in the joint session 'Word from the Ethics and Scientific Advisors'. The presentation argues that governance readiness, in ethics, in regulation, and in data, is a precondition for clinical translation rather than a downstream concern, and that the question is the readiness of the institutions asked to review and oversee this research rather than the properties of any single tool. It sets out the governance position of a Crimean-Congo haemorrhagic fever (CCHF) vaccine programme at the point where a candidate has been through a first-in-human trial in the predecessor project and the next phase is in prospect: material and data crossing nine countries, three of them outside the European Union; artificial intelligence tools whose regulatory and ethics status is unsettled entering the safety analysis pipeline; and consent taken for convalescent sampling rather than for what the samples now support. It poses three governance questions for the consortium, on data sovereignty, on the status of an output when an artificial intelligence tool flags a safety signal, and on the architecture of consent. It identifies four instruments already available for deliberate application to CCHF: the guidance of the EOSC-Future/RDA AI and Data Visitation Working Group (AIDV-WG) together with Global Ethics and Regulatory Preparedness (GERP); the African Vaccine Regulatory Forum (AVRF) and the African Medicines Agency (AMA), with the direction of travel toward one world, one dossier; monitored emergency use of unregistered and investigational interventions (MEURI) and the Ebola ring vaccination trial in Guinea in 2015; and the Ethics, Legal, and Societal Impact (ELSI) Working Group of the Human Genome Project II (HGP2). It closes with three asks of the consortium: that the HGP2 ELSI Working Group be named a governance partner in the next phase of the CCHFVACIM protocol, that a working group session map CCHFVACIM data flows to existing ethics and regulatory frameworks, and that a CCHFVACIM governance annex to the GERP protocol be co-authored.

items.title: Where Do Legal Factors Live in LLMs?
items.abstract: In case-based legal reasoning, legal professionals identify legally significant fact patterns in a new dispute and compare them with those of decided cases. In AI & Law, HYPO dimensions and CATO factors represent these patterns symbolically, organizing expert knowledge distilled from case narratives as explicit, structured, interpretable, and auditable legal concepts and relations that support case comparison, legal argument, and precedent-based reasoning. Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used for legal tasks, yet their internal organization of legal knowledge remains difficult to trace. We investigate whether LLMs form internal representations corresponding to all 26 CATO factors. Two research questions examine linear decodability and sparse localization with sparse autoencoders. Experiments cover three open models, Qwen3-1.7B, Qwen3-8B, and Gemma-2 2B, supported by cross-model comparison and human audit of controlled natural-language passages. Results show that all 26 factors are linearly decodable in all three models. Single-feature sparse readouts cover the complete factor catalog, with best-layer test AUCs ranging from 0.86 to 1.00. Five selected features approach full-vector readout performance. We report 78 model-specific layer-feature coordinates, one for each factor in each model. Together, these results show that information corresponding to expert-defined legal factors can be read from the internal activations of LLMs processing legal narratives. By locating these readouts, our study connects legal language and the symbolic abstractions of HYPO and CATO to learned internal representations.

items.title: Why Customers Welcome or Resist AI Salespeople: Formation Mechanisms of Algorithm Aversion and Algorithm Appreciation in Large Language Model Sales
items.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) now answer product questions, recommend items and help close deals in online shops, banks and telecom services. Customers react to these AI sales agents in two opposite ways. Some avoid them, a pattern researchers call algorithm aversion, while others prefer them to human advice, a pattern called algorithm appreciation. This paper reviews the main empirical studies on both patterns and asks how each one forms when the "algorithm" is a conversational sales agent. Drawing on research in judgment and decision making, consumer behavior and human computer interaction, it proposes a framework with three layers. The first layer contains the cues that an LLM sales agent gives off. The second layer contains five psychological pathways that operate during the conversation: competence belief, error sensitivity, empathy and uniqueness concern, social presence, and perceived control. The third layer contains situational conditions such as product type, the timing of AI identity disclosure, the customer's emotional state and prior AI experience. Six propositions are derived. The paper argues that aversion and appreciation are not fixed traits of customers but outcomes of how these layers combine in a particular sales encounter, and it discusses implications for firms and for future student research.

items.title: Why Do LLMs Accept Generics? Explaining Acceptability using Psycholinguistic and Model-Derived Factors
items.abstract: Psycholinguistic studies explore why humans accept some generic statements but reject others by showing that these judgments depend on more than how common a property is. People consider several other factors such as how well it sets the kind apart from others or whether it is characteristic of the kind. Inspired by the linguistic and cognitive literature, we explore to what extent factors from these studies explain how large language models (LLMs) judge generics. Our results with twelve models on a psycholinguistic dataset and on naturally occurring generics show that models weigh how common a property is against how well it distinguishes the kind, and combine the two much as people do, though less clearly. Like people, they favor characteristic properties, but unlike the accounts of human judgment, they ignore striking ones. What matters most to LLMs is whether a statement is factually true, and much of the influence of human factors reaches their ratings through that judgment. In six 7-9B models, shifting the hidden states along each factor's direction moves the judgment as the factor predicts.

items.abstract: AI-generated images linked to news events and online claims can mislead audiences, enable fraud, or cause public controversy. We introduce WildAIGC-Bench, built through recurring collection across news websites, fact-checking sources, and related social media content. The pipeline combines broad coverage, timely updates, and human-verified labels through scheduled discovery, automatic screening and preliminary annotation, and human review of image-specific evidence. The benchmark contains 407 verified AI-generated or edited images, each accompanied by a source webpage link and an evidence summary. Images retain the conditions encountered online, including compression, screenshots, and recapture. Evaluation of dedicated visual detectors, multimodal large language models, and a simple Perception Encoder baseline reveals substantial recall gaps relative to existing benchmarks. WildAIGC-Bench provides both a practical detection challenge and a basis for continued data expansion and source-based verification. The dataset is released at https://github.com/YuZijian/WildAIGC-Bench.
topics: Generative Adversarial Networks and Image Synthesis

items.title: Writing a Thesis in the age of GenAI and Open Science
items.abstract: Slides of a lecture given at the AIOS multiplier event (Bologna, 20 October 2026, online), addressed mainly to Computer Science students preparing a thesis. The lecture discusses how generative AI changes each stage of a thesis, from literature search to writing, and how Open Science practices make the resulting work inspectable, reproducible and reusable. A hypothetical running example, a thesis on LLM-assisted unit test generation, illustrates research questions and related work, research design and decision logs, effectiveness metrics (mutation score, coverage, defect detection, effort), FAIR principles, Software Heritage and reproducibility packages. The lecture also covers the independent verification of AI output and the competences a thesis requires (DigComp, ResearchComp, ESCO). It ends with a checklist for students. The final part is self-critical: it examines how the lecture itself was prepared and where it failed to follow its own Open Science advice. It closes with an Open Science statement for the lecture.

items.title: ¿Hasta dónde delegar? Una propuesta ético-metodológica para el uso de IA generativa en investigación cualitativa en salud y cuidados
items.abstract: Introduction: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) has increased its presence in qualitative research studies. These tools bring opportunities and risks that need to be considered because of the type of information involved in studies with human participants. Objective: To present a proposal that contributes to the discussion of the tasks in which AI may intervene without putting methodological and ethical principles at risk. Method: Critical and focused review of literature published between 2023 and 2026, a period in which the use of language models expanded in qualitative research. The material was organized according to the use of models, the type of information, the human decisions made during the process, and ethical considerations. Results: The analysis made it possible to define four dimensions for making decisions about the use of technology: methodological coherence, proximity to the interpretive core, exposure of information, and the verifiability of technological involvement. These dimensions were used to create a three-level traffic-light system for the use of these technologies. Conclusions: The use of AI does not depend only on the model being used. Human participation and responsibility are needed to ensure methodological coherence, protect confidential information, and verify and trace findings against the original corpus. The researcher is responsible for every decision made throughout the entire process.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

items.title: ‘Let’s work alongside it’: healthcare professionals’ perspectives of generative AI in supporting care at home in paediatric rheumatology
items.abstract: Objectives Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is increasingly explored in healthcare, yet its potential to support care at home remains largely unexamined. In paediatric rheumatology, where families frequently undertake complex tasks to manage treatment plans between appointments, safe and effective guidance is essential. The aim of the current study was to understand healthcare professionals' (HCPs') views on adopting GenAI tools to help families manage their child's care. Methods Utilising a vignette-based methodology, paediatric rheumatology HCPs were invited to focus groups and presented with 3 hypothetical scenarios: (1) injection administration, (2) flare assessment, and (3) physiotherapy exercises. Following the principles outlined by Braun and Clarke, data were analysed using thematic analysis. Results A total of 37 HCPs from the wider multidisciplinary team from 14 different hospitals participated in this study. Six main themes were identified: (1) opportunities of GenAI to benefit patient care; (2) disadvantages and challenges; (3) risks, safety netting, and evaluation; (4) different approaches of utilising GenAI; (5) role of HCPs in the world of GenAI; and (6) ensuring inclusivity and accessibility. Conclusions HCPs recognised opportunities for how GenAI could support caregivers in managing their child's healthcare or young people's self-management, particularly through guidance support rather than clinical interpretation. However, concerns were raised regarding the accuracy, reliability, privacy, and data governance of currently existing GenAI tools. The perspectives of HCPs are critical to ensuring that the application of GenAI in healthcare aligns with clinical expectations, ethical standards, regulatory processes, and the needs of patients and families.

items.title: "Artificial Intelligence in The Indian Banking Sector: A Strategic Tool for Enhancing Human Resource Utilization, Reducing Non-Performing Assets, Improving Profitability, Marketing Effectiveness, And Cyber Security – A Comparative Study of Scheduled Public Sector Banks, Private Sector Banks and Cooperative Banks (2020–2025)"
items.abstract: The Indian banking industry is undergoing a paradigm shift driven by rapid technological advancements, digital transformation, and evolving customer expectations. Artificial Intelligence (AI), as a subset of advanced digital technologies, has emerged as a transformative force capable of redefining banking operations across all segments of the financial system. Scheduled Public Sector Banks, Private Sector Banks, and Cooperative Banks are increasingly adopting AI-based applications to improve operational efficiency, customer service, credit appraisal, fraud detection, cybersecurity, human resource management, and marketing effectiveness. AI enables banks to analyze large volumes of structured and unstructured data in real time, automate repetitive processes, predict customer behavior, and enhance decision-making with greater accuracy and speed.Over the last five financial years (FY 2020–FY 2025), the Indian banking sector has demonstrated significant improvement in financial health. Gross Non-Performing Assets (GNPAs) have declined to multi-year lows, while profitability has reached record levels due to strengthened risk management, improved governance, digital banking initiatives, and regulatory reforms introduced by the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) and the Government of India. AI has played an increasingly important role by enabling predictive analytics for credit risk assessment, early warning systems for loan defaults, automated compliance monitoring, personalized customer engagement, and intelligent cybersecurity mechanisms.This research paper examines the effectiveness of AI adoption across different categories of Indian banks, with special emphasis on its impact on human resource utilization, reduction of NPAs, profitability enhancement, marketing strategies, fraud prevention, and cybersecurity resilience. The study adopts a descriptive and analytical research design based on secondary data collected from RBI publications, Government reports, annual reports of major banks, and academic literature. Comparative analysis is undertaken using financial indicators from leading Public Sector Banks, Private Sector Banks, and Cooperative Banks during the period 2020–2025.The study concludes that AI has significantly improved operational efficiency, customer satisfaction, and financial performance in the Indian banking industry. However, challenges relating to data privacy, ethical AI, infrastructure costs, shortage of skilled manpower, algorithmic transparency, and regulatory compliance continue to constrain widespread adoption, particularly among Cooperative Banks. The paper recommends the development of a comprehensive national AI strategy for banking, enhanced investment in digital infrastructure, employee upskilling, standardized AI governance frameworks, and collaborative initiatives between regulators, banks, fintech firms, and academic institutions.

items.title: “I Just Needed Someone to Listen”: A Community Discussion Analysis of Redditors’ Discourse About Using General-Purpose LLMs for Therapy
items.abstract: Despite increasing efforts of legislatures to prohibit specialized AI-driven apps from providing therapeutic decision-making, general-purpose Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly being used as alternative tools for mental health support. In this paper, we examine the increased adoption of AI for mental health through the lens of proponents’ and opponents’ discussions on public forums. Through a qualitative analysis of 67 Reddit discussion threads (totaling 2948 comments), we offer an in-depth investigation of the various contexts in which users rely on (or fail to rely on) AI for mental health support, as well as an analysis of the main discussions (including positions for and against the use of AI for therapy) within the community. By critically reflecting on our findings, we highlight ethical considerations and discuss how research, design and regulation of AI tools can help improve mental health support for users with complicated needs while mitigating potential harms.

items.title: A blessing or a curse? The impact of artificial intelligence innovation on corporate energy efficiency
items.abstract: This study examines how artificial intelligence (AI) innovation influences corporate energy efficiency and the underlying mechanisms. We develop a general equilibrium model incorporating energy input and endogenous AI technology to explain how AI innovation improves energy efficiency through production process optimization. Using a deep-learning-based text identification, we develop a firm-level measure of AI innovation for Chinese listed companies over the period 2008–2022. Our empirical results show that AI innovation significantly improves corporate energy efficiency, while the mechanism analysis provides evidence consistent with production process optimization as an important transmission channel. This positive effect is stronger among firms operating in key technological sectors and capital-intensive industries. Further, we find that disruptive AI innovation produces a larger effect than general AI innovation. We also document that local governments' attention to AI development and intra-firm data sharing strengthen the energy-efficiency gains associated with AI innovation. This study contributes to research on digital innovation and firm sustainability by showing how AI-driven innovation translates into efficiency-enhancing outcomes through organizational and data-governance mechanisms.

items.title: A Conceptual Framework and Ontological Classification for the Intelligent Design of Agri-Food SME Plant Layouts Under Industry 5.0
items.abstract: Facility layout planning (FLP) in the agri-food sector faces unique complexities due to product perishability, biosafety regulations, and Industry 5.0 (I5.0) requirements. The reviewed literature is skewed toward static formulations that overlook detailed layout, demand uncertainty, and social sustainability. In response, a targeted review, reported following PRISMA 2020, and expert judgement yielded an ontological classification of ten characteristics influencing detailed agri-food layouts, whose relevance and relationships were supported by five external experts (S-CVI/Ave = 0.96); the system roles proposed by the authors were not reproduced in a blind assignment and remain modelling hypotheses. We then develop an eight-pillar conceptual framework addressing dynamic multi-period planning, stochastic uncertainty, multi-objective optimisation, comprehensive sustainability, human-centric ergonomics, operation-level routing, a bottom-up approach, and perishability as an endogenous variable. A diagnostic case study of an agri-food small and medium-sized enterprise (SME) illustrates how the classification structures the diagnosis of layout inefficiencies, such as products reaching customers with reduced shelf life. Aligned with I5.0 principles, this research provides a conceptual basis for models that treat perishability and human well-being as core design variables. The classification applies mainly to agri-food SMEs operating under make-to-order and just-in-time strategies; large make-to-stock manufacturers should also consider product homogeneity and storage-based product types.

items.title: A cross-sectional study on the perceptions, utilization, and educational needs of medical students regarding AI, 3D PDF, and deep learning
items.abstract: This study aimed to evaluate undergraduate medical students’ awareness, use, perceived competence, and educational expectations regarding artificial intelligence (AI), three-dimensional portable document format (3D PDF), and deep learning in anatomy education. Data from 607 valid questionnaire responses were analyzed using descriptive statistics and chi-square tests of independence. Awareness of AI tools was high, with ChatGPT being the most recognized platform, followed by Gemini and OpenAI. Students mainly used AI to acquire theoretical knowledge, and AI use during studying anatomy ( p = 0.012). The frequency of AI use also varied according to both gender ( p = 0.028) and grade ( p = 0.010). Students reported a need for support in technical use, reliability checks, and ethical principles. Self-rated AI competence was generally moderate and differed significantly by gender ( p < 0.001). Deep learning was less familiar than AI and 3D PDFs. The use of 3D PDFs differed significantly by gender ( p = 0.025) and grade ( p = 0.028). Students considered 3D PDFs most applicable to anatomy education, followed by medical imaging and surgical planning ( p < 0.001). Overall, the findings indicate high digital awareness among medical students but limited structured preparation for responsible AI use, deep learning literacy, and visualization-based anatomical learning. items.abstract: ABSTRACT This article examines a document that the ChatGPT interface made available during an exchange about capacity for saved memories. The response presented the reorganisation of writing rules for a narrative project as already completed, although my request concerned capacity alone, and no recorded prompt requested a file or specified the proposed hierarchy. Earlier, I had copied every visible saved memory entry verbatim into another document, allowing comparison in both directions to identify corresponding formulations and changes in their placement or prescriptive force. The phenomenological account follows my remembered reading and remains separate from those findings. In the linked document, rules appeared within a hierarchy not specified in my request and reading those formulations in their new positions changed how I understood decisions. Available records establish the limited request and the sequence through which the organised file became available without identifying the operations that produced the file. In this case, I formulated the rules without articulating their comprehensive relations, and recognising my formulations did not mean understanding what their new placement asserted. ChatGPT presented the organisation as already complete, whereas a human collaborator could have presented the same arrangement together with reasons.

Este artigo investiga os impactos do ruído comunicacional na percepção de risco dos trabalhadores operacionais e propõe estratégias de simplificação e dinamização das mensagens corporativas. Por meio de uma pesquisa bibliográfico-qualitativa, analisa-se a aplicação do microlearning, do design de informação e do Diálogo Diário de Segurança (DDS) interativo como alternativas ao modelo tradicional de sobrecarga informativa. ABSTRACT: The excess of communication stimuli in the industrial environment has generated the phenomenon of information fatigue, compromising the retention of vital Occupational Health and Safety (OHS) guidelines. This article investigates the impacts of communication noise on operational workers' risk perception and proposes strategies for simplifying and streamlining corporate messages. Through qualitative-bibliographic research, the application of microlearning, information design, and interactive Daily Safety Dialogues (DDS) is analyzed as alternatives to the traditional model of information overload. It concludes that objectivity, visual clarity, and interactivity are essential to break through employee desensitization, ensuring that risk alerts are properly assimilated and put into practice.

items.title: A GenAI-supported job interview training robot for young adults with special education needs
items.abstract: Background and aims Employment opportunities for young adults with special education needs (YA-SEN) are often less favourable compared to their peers without SEN. They are often anxious during interviews, especially when answering open-ended questions with unfamiliar interviewers and unexpected interruptions occur. To fill the gap, we developed an interactive job interview training (JIT) system featuring a cat-shaped robot – JIT-bot.Sample JIT-bot was designed to provide an engaging, adaptive, and personalised training experience that supported users to practice and refine their interviewing skills in a less stressful environment. We recruited 28 participants in our study.Methods A mixed-method approach was employed, including proficiency tests, interviews, and questionnaires.Results Results provided preliminary evidence that the experimental group showed a statistically significant improvement in intrinsic motivation. In contrast, the behavioural engagement of the control group decreased slightly. These findings and feedback will suggest future enhancements to JIT-bot’s features and functions, making it a valuable tool to support JIT for YA-SEN.

items.title: A large-scale comparison of human and large language model raters in automated essay scoring
items.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have brought about pivotal changes in writing assessment, particularly through comparisons with human raters. Nevertheless, most current studies are limited to analyzes that compare a small number of models with human raters and focus primarily on overall score differences or inter-rater agreement. This quantitative study compares 17 cutting-edge LLMs on the same dataset, examining the models’ scoring consistency, proximity to the mean scores assigned by human raters, and structural similarity and clustering analyzes of scoring behaviours relative to those of humans, based on analytic sub-dimensions, using a multidimensional approach. To that end, the research analyzed literary essays written by 46 first-year students at upper-intermediate proficiency in the English Language and Literature department of a state university in Türkiye, based on Ernest Hemingway's short story ‘The Cat in the Rain,’ using an expert-validated six-dimensional analytic rubric. The findings reveal substantial variability at the level of analytic sub-dimensions among 17 LLMs despite their proximity to experts in terms of overall scores. Moreover, these models clustered according to their average dimension-score profiles, while some displayed closer alignment with human rater profiles. Finally, while different correlation values were identified for each analytic dimension, high consistency was noted between the two expert raters with respect to overall scoring.

items.title: A Managed Database-as-a-Service Platform for Scientific Computing
items.abstract: Scientific computing at HPC facilities increasingly relies on database infrastructure across a growing range of workloads: vector search and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), structured analytics, and AI-driven knowledge discovery over community corpora spanning documentation, experimental datasets, simulation outputs, and literature collections. These corpora are inherently shared facility resources, serving researchers, facility support staff, and AI agents across projects and institutions. Yet the supporting infrastructure remains built per project: each team provisions, configures, and operates its own database instance, with no facility-level registry, no shared identity layer, and no uniform interface for discovering or accessing the databases hosted across the facility. Commercial cloud platforms have addressed analogous needs through managed Database-as-a-Service offerings (e.g., Amazon RDS, Snowflake, Pinecone). However, these solutions do not transfer cleanly to scientific computing: they rely on proprietary identity systems, cannot directly access facility filesystems, and incur substantial data egress costs. We are building the missing piece: a managed database platform that lives inside the HPC facility, developed and evaluated on ALCF Polaris. One federated sign-in (Globus) brings a researcher — or an AI agent acting on their behalf — to every database the facility hosts, through a web UI, a scriptable API, or the Model Context Protocol. Governance, catalog, and access control are handled once by the platform and inherited by every project by default. The central design choice is scaling, native to HPC. Each workload is decomposed into its resource-consuming stages, and each stage can be scaled independently across nodes. As one representative example, a vector-search workload scales GPU-based embedding generation and search-index serving independently across nodes, reaching 5,197 queries/sec on 8 nodes (4.3× single-node) on ALCF Polaris and still climbing at maximum tested concurrency. Governance adds modest overhead at single-user load and becomes negligible under concurrency. In an end-to-end RAG pipeline built on this workload, retrieval contributes under 2% of total latency — the bottleneck has moved entirely to LLM generation. The same decomposition pattern is designed to extend to other workload types as additional engine adapters are integrated. The talk presents what changes when scientific data services are native to the facility: who can use them, what AI agents become capable of, and how a single platform can replace per-project infrastructure across an entire lab. We will share the design tradeoffs, what the scaling numbers mean for facility capacity planning, and the next stage of the design — co-locating the database service with model-inference services and scaling both on demand against shared facility resources, planned for the coming year. We invite peer facilities to adopt the platform and collaborate with us on a unified, cross-facility scientific data service.

items.title: A Multi-Agent AI System for Automating Tokamak-Plasma Simulation for Nuclear Fusion Energy.
items.abstract: Building a correct, performant HPC simulation from a scientific idea demands scarce, largely implicit expertise in numerical methods and library APIs. AI agents can now draft such code, but a draft that looks right is not necessarily one that an engineer can trust. We take a research-software-engineering (RSE) view of a real fusion-energy problem: not whether AI can replace that expertise, but what an RSE must build around a multi-agent AI system (orchestration, verification gates, provenance, and guardrails) to make its output trustworthy. Using a multi-agent AI system, from a plain-language prompt, we generate a PETSc simulation of the tokamak Grad–Shafranov equilibrium for nuclear fusion energy. In this poster, we will present the PETSc multi-agent system and demonstrate its application on this problem. The system includes a mathematical modeling agent, a numerical analysis agent, and an HPC code generation and execution agent. Around them, there is a project-owned orchestration driver that records every artifact (model, discretization decision, generated source code, build / run logs) with full provenance, so that runs are reproducible, resumable, and auditable. There is also a verification harness that gates every result before it is accepted. From the prompt (“Grad–Shafranov equilibrium for magnetically confined plasma in a tokamak”), the mathematical modeling agent identified the governing equation and returned its strong and weak forms; the numerical analysis agent selected a nonlinear solver on a structured grid; and the HPC code generation and execution agent produced a compact PETSc program that discretizes the operator on a distributed array with a true Jacobian matrix, and embeds a method-of-manufactured-solutions check. We do not treat “it compiled and ran” as sufficient evidence of success: an MPI-parallel grid-refinement study confirms second-order convergence. Verification, not the model’s confidence, decides acceptance. The same pipeline then produced one parameterized solver for several real-machine-shaped equilibria. Each was verified against an exact analytic benchmark and cross-checked against an independent community code. We scaled from the toy anchor to trustworthy shaped cases without re-architecting the generated solver. Running the AI agents on a shared HPC machine took environment and dependency wrangling, working-directory-independent process spawning, and graceful degradation when optional components were absent. There are also guardrails: in one instructive failure, a hard-coded iteration cap in the built-in orchestrator mislabeled a genuinely successful multi-stage run as a failure. We diagnosed it and contributed the fix upstream. Human effort is not eliminated but relocated, from writing solver code to engineering the orchestration, verification, and guardrails that make an AI system’s output trustworthy and its failures legible. We report per-run decision-gate metrics: correctness (model identified, program compiled and ran, convergence order), efficiency (execution duration, LLM / tool calls), and where human effort went (as a lightweight, reusable way to evaluate an agentic workflow rather than merely admire its output). The contribution is a candid, verification-driven account of how a research software engineer can wrap multi-agent AI code generation so that it produces trustworthy HPC simulation code for a flagship fusion-energy problem, and of the guardrails needed when it does not. In future work, we will raise the simulation difficulty to nonlinear profiles, time-dependent and resistive magnetohydrodynamics, and three-dimensional tokamak plasma, to map where the system succeeds and where it breaks, and to design guardrails and human-in-the-loop checkpoints that keep engineers in control as problems get harder.

items.title: A new approach to observing intuition during crisis exercises: linguistic markers of cognitive heuristics
items.abstract: Organisations are using crisis exercises to train their crisis management staff. Few studies have examined intuitive decision-making during exercises, which manifests itself in the form of heuristics: cognitive shortcuts. Identifying these heuristics duringobservation of exercises is complex due to the lack of a methodology for considering heuristics during exercises. To overcome this problem, we propose a methodology for observing linguistic markers to identify heuristics during 32 crisis exercises at the French Alternative Energies and Atomic Energy Commission. This research has shown that our methodology provides a framework for identifying seven specific heuristics during crisis exercises. We conclude the article with the contributions of our methodology and prospects for further development.

items.title: A novel cloud-enabled enterprise information systems framework for accelerating digital transformation strategies
items.abstract: The co-evolution of micro-frontend UIs and backend microservices in cloud-native environments is complicated by UI–API semantic drift, dynamic workloads, and safe-deployment constraints. A tripartite agentic AI framework is introduced that combines reinforcement-learning (RL) agents for adaptive runtime control, large-language-model (LLM) synthesizers for automated artifact generation, and policy-as-code governors for security and compliance enforcement. The co-evolution process is formulated as a drift-aware Markov decision process, while Kubernetes-native traffic shifting supports progressive rollout and rollback. KubeSim was used for offline policy training; the reported performance results were obtained from live AWS EKS, Google GKE, and Azure AKS clusters. Across five benchmarks, the framework achieved a mean resolution success rate of 91.4%, compared with 62.0% for rule-based control, 71.1% for a controlled zero-shot LLM baseline, and 79.0% for partial RL. The framework also reduced normalized mean time to recovery by 80%, normalized change failure rate by 75%, and CPU utilization by 30 percentage points, while attaining a 98% audit pass rate. Component-removal and counterfactual-return analyses indicate complementary contributions from adaptive control, artifact synthesis, and policy enforcement. These results support the effectiveness, scalability, and governability of the framework for cloud-native enterprise digital transformation.

items.title: A Paradox Perspective
items.abstract: This chapter investigates how artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping medical professionalism, drawing on paradox theory, particularly the automation-augmentation paradox, to analyse how medical work is being redefined. While the medical profession has historically been able to balance resistance and adaptation to external pressures, AI represents a qualitatively different challenge: it encroaches on core professional expertise, introduces new knowledge agents into clinical decision-making, and disrupts traditional power structures between doctors, patients, and clinical knowledge. This chapter discusses how current AI deployments predominantly augment medical judgement, especially in specialties such as radiology, cardiology, and neurology. Yet the trajectory of AI integration suggests an evolving interplay between augmentation and automation, requiring clinicians to strategically engage with technologies that both complement and potentially transform their expertise. A central focus is on how AI might help address longstanding cognitive and implicit biases in medical decision-making related to race, gender, age, disability, and socioeconomic status. Although AI offers opportunities to reduce inequities, it also risks replicating or amplifying them due to biased training data, design choices, and opaque algorithms. This chapter argues for a hybrid model of medical doctor-AI collaboration that leverages mutual learning, preserves professional responsibility, and embeds safeguards to mitigate bias.

items.abstract: Conflicts of interest: No conflicts of interest Sources of funding: No funding obtained Background Low back pain is the leading cause of years lived with disability worldwide and consequently it is the most common condition treated by physiotherapists in an out-patient setting. Physiotherapists also have a role to play in preventing spinal pain by providing ergonomic education. Purpose of Study To compare spinal angles whilst conducting a seated typing task with a self-selected optimal posture. Methods Cross-sectional pilot study. Twenty asymptomatic participants (9 male, 11 female, aged 19 to 23 years) adopted their normal sitting working posture using a laptop to conduct a typing task; they were then asked to adopt what they considered to be their best sitting posture. Retroreflective markers were attached to: L4, ASIS, PSIS, T12, C7, tragus and canthus. Spinal (neck, thoracic, lumbar and pelvic) angles were established via digital photographs using a bespoke MATLAB programme (MathWorks). Statistical analysis (Wilcoxon signed ranks tests) was conducted to determine between condition differences. Results No statistically significant results were observed between conditions for pelvic angles (p>0.05), however statistically significant differences (p<0.05) were observed for lumbar, thoracic and neck angles. In all cases participants adopted more ‘upright’ optimal postures. Conclusion The results suggest that a self-selected optimal posture varies significantly with a computer working posture for lumbar, thoracic and neck angles. Whilst pelvic angles were not significantly different between conditions, descriptive analysis demonstrated a more flexed position for all angles during the working posture. Whilst an optimal posture remains debatable, these differences highlight the need to identify interventions to address differences between working and optimal postures.

items.abstract: This article examines the figure of the first lady as a gender technology and a form of communicational mediation in Brazilian politics, challenging the androcentric canon of Political Communication. Drawing on feminist epistemology, situated knowledges, and the concept of coloniality of gender, it explores how gendered regimes of visibility co-produce authority, legitimacy, and recognition. Through an analysis of the Instagram profiles of Rosângela “Janja” Lula da Silva and Michelle Bolsonaro, the study investigates the sociotechnical architectures that organize processes of validation, surveillance, and disciplining of bodies. It argues that the first lady operates as a symbolic infrastructure of the political system within platformized communication environments.

items.title: A Proposed Model for Teachers' AI Competencies Based on UNESCO and DigCompEdu Frameworks: A Qualitative Study
items.abstract: Teachers’ competencies in artificial intelligence (AI) constitute a fundamental element for achieving innovative and effective education aligned with the demands of the twenty-first century. This study aims to propose a comprehensive model of teachers’ AI competencies based on the UNESCO AI Competency Framework for Teachers and the European Digital Competence Framework for Educators (DigCompEdu), while adapting them to suit the needs of teacher preparation programs in faculties of education. The study adopts a qualitative approach using focus groups with experts in curriculum and instruction as well as educational technology. The domains, standards, and indicators of both frameworks were analyzed and discussed in order to derive a practical and contextually relevant model. The study resulted in a proposed model comprising five main domains, 15 standards, and 48 performance indicators, covering cognitive, pedagogical, ethical, professional, and assessment dimensions. It also provides practical recommendations for developing teacher preparation and continuous professional development programs, with a focus on integrating artificial intelligence in a responsible and effective manner to support interactive and inclusive learning for students.

items.title: A Return to Natural Human Learning in the Age of AI: Active Agency, Applied Curiosity and a Human-Governed Architecture for Augmented Understanding
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence is frequently described as if increasing computational capability were equivalent to increasing intelligence. This article rejects that scalar assumption and repositions artificial systems within a broader account of Natural Human Learning. It synthesises the 2026 Benjamin et al. work on cCC*, agency, bounded choice, Socialwork*, AEIOUF and consciousing; the Benjamin-McLaughlin account of Applied Curiosity and Augmented Understanding; the Benjamin-Palmer development of W-ALL as an externalised, revisable learning field; and the Natural Learning triptych's account of embodied, pre-verbal and AI-age learning. The synthesis is named LUMO: a human-governed learning environment in which machine generation enlarges the field of chances without displacing human authorship of choices, changes, responsibility or meaning. The paper advances four connected claims. First, learning begins before artificial representation - and before language: natural processes, embodiment, neural dynamics, encounter and difference provide the "horse" before the computational "cart". Second, uniquely human active agency (AAA) is categorical rather than scalar: capability may increase, but agency is not made "super" by more computation. Third, cCC* (Curiosity → Chances → Choices → Changes) is operationalised through the sequential AEIOUF process, A → E → I → O → U → F, with Conative Situational Integration (CSI) maintaining continuity across transitions. Fourth, LUMO should be coupled to protected canonical infrastructure: LUMO supports porous exploration; LIMO, with PROTON guardrails, protects provenance, permissions, canonical state and authorised change. R1-R16 and the 96-facet R × AEIOUF address space provide a selective-context routing layer, while CQI and CGI distinguish inquiry from generative construction. In the age of AI, the binding criterion becomes the preservation of the learner's CAN before externally supplied COULD. The resulting architecture reframes AI as a contingent support to human Natural Learning rather than its model, endpoint or successor. Sixteen research propositions are specified for empirical evaluation.

items.title: A Situation Monitoring, Analysis, and Reporting Team (SMART) framework for structuring Situational Awareness (SA) in construction projects
items.abstract: Construction projects are socio-technical systems requiring shared Situation Awareness (SA) to manage uncertainty and change. This study proposes Situation Monitoring, Analysis, and Reporting Teams (SMART) as a human-centred framework for structuring shared SA in construction. A thematic literature review identified a gap in understanding SA as an ongoing socio-technical process. An exploratory pilot study in a simulated modular construction setting examines communication patterns across four reporting phases: no reporting, self-reporting, SMART reporting, and post-intervention. SMART reporting was associated with a shift from fragmented to more structured and task-oriented communication, alongside increased information sharing and task-related exchanges. These patterns indicate coordination and information exchange, not direct measures of SA. The study makes three contributions: (1) reconceptualizing SA as an organizational socio-technical process rather than an individual or technology-driven outcome; (2) introducing SMART as a mechanism linking monitoring, sensemaking, and reporting; and (3) providing exploratory evidence that structured reporting is associated with communication patterns linked to SA processes. The controlled pilot setting and use of proxy indicators bounds findings. Future research should test SMART in real-world scenarios and examine its integration with digital and AI-assisted tools.

items.title: A socio-computational framework for evaluating artificial intelligence adoption readiness in small-scale businesses
items.abstract: Purpose Adoption of artificial intelligence (AI) across small-scale businesses remains uneven even with the growing pace of digital transformation. Large enterprises are rapidly integrating AI into their operations, while there is still a barrier to adoption within small-scale businesses. This study proposes and examines an exploratory computational readiness index (CRI) that brings together behavioral, organizational and environmental dimensions to understand the preparedness of small-scale businesses in adopting AI. This index is offered as a preliminary firm-level diagnostic rather than a fully validated measure. Design/methodology/approach A quantitative, multi-source design was used, combining primary survey data from small-scale businesses with secondary global data collected from international sources and informal conversations with additional small business owners, managers and employees who fell outside the formal survey sample. Survey instruments were used to capture behavioral, organizational and environmental factors influencing the decision to adopt AI. This was also complemented with secondary global data collected and combined to derive the readiness index. Appropriate statistical tests were conducted to examine relationships among key dimensions and the overall readiness index. Findings Organizational factors like employee skills, motivation and opportunities were most consistently linked with readiness across groups, followed by individuals’ behavioral factors. External factors such as infrastructure and environment appeared to have comparatively smaller influence. The results of the study have been used to develop a readiness index that is intended to indicate the extent to which a small-scale business may be prepared to adopt AI. Practical implications The CRI proposed in this study can become a practical tool for policymakers and leaders within small-scale businesses for readiness assessment, prioritizing capability building within the organization rather than focusing on infrastructure investments alone. Originality/value This study contributes to the literature by proposing a novel framework for assessing AI readiness in small-scale businesses, integrating human, organizational and environmental dimensions.

items.title: A Standardized Benchmarking Framework for the Automated Evaluation of AI-Generated Travel Plans
items.abstract: The rapid adoption of large language models (LLMs) transformed the way users obtained travel recommendations and generated personalized travel plans. However, standardized methods for comparing AI-generated travel itineraries across heterogeneous providers remained limited. This study presented the design, implementation, and experimental evaluation of a web-based benchmarking framework for the standardized and automated comparison of AI-generated travel plans. The framework integrated standardized prompt generation, structured JSON response processing, field-level comparison, deterministic rule-based scoring, model ranking, and exportable benchmarking reports. It was evaluated across three travel-planning scenarios involving Prague, Rome, and Tokyo, with three independent benchmark executions attempted for each scenario, resulting in 27 provider-level requests. Eight executions produced complete three-provider comparisons; one Rome execution was incomplete because Microsoft Phi returned malformed JSON. Across the eight complete executions, Gemini achieved a mean structural-completeness score of 57.00/57 (SD = 0.00), ChatGPT achieved 47.38/57 (SD = 3.02), and Microsoft Phi achieved 34.63/57 (SD = 5.26), with the same rank ordering observed in all complete comparisons. Supplementary constraint-compliance analysis demonstrated that structural completeness did not necessarily imply full satisfaction of travel requirements. Sustainability-related outputs were additionally examined as a separate dimension. The results demonstrated consistent framework operation under the tested scenarios and repetitions while emphasizing the need to distinguish structural completeness from constraint compliance, factual accuracy, practical feasibility, and sustainability-related performance.

items.title: A Study on the Adoption and Responsible Use of Generative AI Tools for Sustainable Learning among Undergraduate Students
items.abstract: Abstract Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) has emerged as a transformative technology in higher education, significantly influencing the way students learn, access information, complete academic tasks, and develop professional skills. Tools such as ChatGPT, Google Gemini, Microsoft Copilot, and Canva AI have become increasingly popular among commerce students for assignments, presentations, exam preparation, and concept clarification. While these technologies offer opportunities for personalized and efficient learning, their growing use also raises concerns regarding academic integrity, ethical practices, critical thinking, and dependency on AI-generated content. This study aims to examine the adoption and responsible use of Generative AI tools among commerce students in higher education and to evaluate their contribution towards sustainable learning. The research adopts a descriptive and analytical research design using primary data collected through a structured questionnaire administered to commerce students. The study focuses on students' awareness of GenAI tools, frequency and purpose of usage, responsible AI practices, AI dependency, and the perceived impact of AI on academic productivity and sustainable learning outcomes. The study is expected to provide insights into how commerce students integrate Generative AI into their academic learning and whether they use these tools responsibly by verifying information, avoiding plagiarism, and using AI as a learning aid rather than a substitute for independent thinking. It also explores the relationship between AI adoption, ethical usage, and sustainable learning practices in the context of higher education. The findings of this research are expected to assist educators, higher education institutions, and policymakers in designing AI literacy initiatives, promoting responsible AI usage, and developing pedagogical practices aligned with the objectives of sustainable and inclusive education. The study contributes to the growing body of literature on Artificial Intelligence in commerce education by emphasizing the importance of balancing technological innovation with ethical responsibility and lifelong learning in higher education. Keywords: Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI), Responsible AI, Sustainable Learning, Commerce Students, Higher Education, AI Ethics, Academic Productivity, Digital Literacy.
